title: [Feature] Add middleware callback with step info before each step is ran
gold_answer: Staff confirmed that `beforeExecution()` fires when the function starts executing new code, not before each step, so it can't report the upcoming step name. They proposed new step-level hooks, `beforeStepExecution()` (with step info) and `afterStepExecution()` (with the result), as a missing piece in middleware. The thread does not show these hooks shipping.
gold_thread:
Hi @mcky! 👋

Ah - this is a perfect use case and something we want to get right for middleware to make sure it's not restrictive. The debugging middleware in #217 is actually entirely middleware (no internals at all), but it's still lacking the accuracy you're wanting here.

The technical detail here is that `beforeExecution()` tracks when we're about to begin executing new code in the function as a whole - not necessarily a new step. In addition, it may be the case that we call the hook, execute the function as a whole, and _then_ decide to run a step in the same execution. Calling the same hook twice would be a bit confusing, I think.

It sounds to me like this might warrant a new hook that clearly marks when we're running a step, like `beforeStepExcecution()` and `afterStepExecution()`.

- Function hooks
  - `beforeExecution()` - starting to execute new code in the function
  - `afterExecution()` - finished executing the function
- Step hooks
  - <kbd>NEW</kbd> `beforeStepExecution()` - starting to execute a step (includes that step info)
  - <kbd>NEW</kbd> `afterStepExecution()` - finished executing the step (includes result, similar to `transformOutput()`)

We've seen this requirement pop up before - I think it may be a missing piece in our hooks right now.

re: p.s. - Yes! 🙌 Diagrams of when these hooks run would be great. I'm thinking a controllable animation that steps over code on one side and hooks on the other might be good. 🤔

cleaned.question: In an Inngest function using step.run, the middleware beforeExecution callback does not expose the name of the step about to execute, so the developer cannot log each step before it runs. The only step-aware hook, transformOutput, runs after the step, which blocks logging before a step and measuring its duration. Is there a middleware hook that receives step info before each step runs, or is this a feature request?

firstDraft.docsGap: The docs don't list the exact fields on `stepInfo` (such as the step display name) or say how the v4 hooks map to the older `beforeExecution` and `transformOutput` hooks.

withDocs.docsGap: The docs don't list the exact fields on `stepInfo` (such as the step display name) or say how the v4 hooks map to the older `beforeExecution` and `transformOutput` hooks.

control.text:
Short answer: in the TS SDK there isn't a dedicated "before each step" hook that receives the step name, so you can't do this cleanly with `beforeExecution` today. Treat the step name gap as a limitation or feature request, not something you're missing.

What exists in the middleware `onFunctionRun` lifecycle (v3):
- `transformInput`: runs when the function is invoked. It gets `ctx` and `steps` (already-memoized step data), but not the step about to run.
- `beforeMemoization` / `afterMemoization`, `beforeExecution` / `afterExecution`: these mark phases of the function run, with no step info.
- `transformOutput`: gets `result` and, for step results, the step info (e.g. `result.step` with its id/name). It runs after the step.
- `finished`, `beforeResponse`: run at the end of the run or request.

Workarounds:
1. Wrap `step.run` yourself. In `transformInput`, return a `ctx` with a wrapped `step` whose `run` logs the name, starts a timer, calls the original, then logs the duration. I'm fairly sure this works, but I haven't verified it against the current SDK types.
2. Use `transformOutput` for after-step logging. Pair it with `beforeExecution` timestamps to approximate durations.
3. Log inside each `step.run` callback.

I'd file a feature request for a per-step hook, e.g. `onStepStart` or `beforeStepExecution`, with the step name and id. Please check the latest SDK release notes first, in case one has been added.
control.docsGap: The middleware docs should state which lifecycle hooks receive step info (name/id) and show how to wrap step.run for per-step timing.
control.whyUnsure: No doc or past fix matched this: answer is from memory of the SDK middleware API and may be outdated.

title: [Feature] Allow creating child loggers, or modifying the parent logger state
gold_answer: Staff said you can already pass your own logger with `.child()` when creating the Inngest client, but the types don't reflect that. They plan to extend the passed logger's type so `.child()` is available in functions. Exposing `logger` inside middleware, which would enable the other proposed approaches, was noted as a limiting factor, with no shipped fix yet.
gold_thread:
Hi, @mcky! 👋

Thanks loads for this detailed write-up.

I believe you _should_ be able to bring your own child-compatible logger if you pass a logger with a `.child()` when creating your client, but aye, types won't reflect that, meaning you don't have access to it. We could perhaps simply extend whatever logger you pass there, ensuring you have all of the usual methods (like `.child()`), then this would be less of a problem.

That feels like the best immediate fix, but you raise some good points about middleware and not having access to everything you need. After the fix above, I guess the limiting factor stopping you achieving any of your listed solutions (without patching) is not being able to access `logger` within the middleware hooks?

The logging itself is, internally, middleware, which currently doesn't appear when creating extra middleware. If you _did_ have access to `logger` within your middleware, you could shim it nicely and have the ability to add tools you're wanting such as `setMeta`.

cleaned.question: A developer using the Inngest TypeScript SDK (inngest-js) asks for a way to create child loggers from the function's `logger` context, or to attach metadata such as transactionId to all logs in a function run. They report that the default logger throws "logger.child not implemented for DefaultLogger" and that ProxyLogger does not forward child(), so they patched the SDK with pnpm patch, and they note the docs' child logger section implies a custom logger with .child() would be used. They also suggest a middleware transformInput hook that returns a child logger on ctx.logger.

firstDraft.text:
Short version: pass a logger that implements `.child()` to the client and the SDK will use it. The `DefaultLogger` is just a console wrapper with no `.child()`, which is why you hit that error. The source you patched is the older v3-era `middleware/logger.ts` [9].

Per the docs, if your logger supports `.child()`, the built-in logging middleware uses it to add function name, event name and run ID to every log automatically [2]. So with pino, winston (wrapped) or similar:

```ts
const inngest = new Inngest({ id: "my-app", logger: pino() });
```

For per-run metadata like `transactionId`, your middleware idea is the supported route. The built-in logger is itself middleware, and you can write your own to customize it [4]. In v4, middleware is class-based (`Middleware.BaseMiddleware`) with a `transformInput` hook [3]. Return a `ctx.logger` from there, built with `baseLogger.child({ transactionId: ctx.event.data.transactionId })`. See the logging middleware example in the v4 middleware examples [4]. I haven't verified the exact `transformInput` return shape, so check that example.

Until then, a simple workaround is a plain logger wrapper, or passing `{ transactionId }` as the first argument on each call.

Also, `internalLogger` only routes SDK-internal logs and doesn't affect `ctx.logger` [1].

If you're on v3, `ProxyLogger` not forwarding `child()` is a real limitation. Upgrading to v4 or using the middleware approach avoids patching.
firstDraft.docsGap: The docs should show how to attach per-run metadata such as a transactionId to ctx.logger via middleware, and should say what happens when the configured logger has no .child().
firstDraft.whyUnsure: Docs only partly cover this: the exact v4 transformInput return shape for overriding ctx.logger isn't shown in the sources.

cleaned.question: Is there support or a plan for using Inngest with SolidStart (the Solid.js meta-framework) applications? The requester wants to use Inngest together with a solid-start app.

firstDraft.text:
I can't confirm a first-party SolidStart handler. The sources don't list one, and I don't know of an `inngest/solid-start` export. I'd verify against the current supported-frameworks list before telling the user either way.

SolidStart doesn't need a dedicated adapter, though. Inngest only needs an HTTP endpoint at `/api/inngest` that handles GET, POST and PUT [2]. For frameworks without an official handler, the docs say you can create a custom handler [3].

SolidStart API routes receive a standard `APIEvent` that includes a Web `Request`. A custom handler can wrap that request. Alternatively, you could mount an officially supported handler, such as Express or Hono, alongside the app.

A custom handler should:
- Set `servePath` to `/api/inngest` [1].
- Pass through the GET, POST and PUT methods [2].
- Return Web `Response` objects.

I haven't tested this in SolidStart. Before sending, please check the supported-frameworks page (/docs/learn/serving-inngest-functions) for a SolidStart entry. I can't tell whether one is planned. For that, point the user to a GitHub issue on inngest-js or to Discord.

cleaned.question: The Inngest agent-kit example "deep-research" fails out of the box with "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'step')" thrown from getStepTools in @inngest/agent-kit (chunk-QBAU6UTA.js), called via AgenticModel.infer, Agent.performInference, Agent.run, and NetworkRun.execute while running simple-agent.ts. The developer is on Node v24.2.0, npm 11.3.0, and macOS Sequoia 15.6.1, running the examples with npm install, npx inngest-cli@latest dev, and npm run dev, and asks whether a version bump is needed.

firstDraft.text:
Most likely yes, it's a version mismatch, not your Node/npm/macOS setup. `getStepTools` reads the step tools from the async context of a running Inngest function. In `AgenticModel.infer`, it gets `undefined` back, so `.step` fails. That happens when `@inngest/agent-kit` and the `inngest` package resolve to incompatible versions. Examples are a v3-era agent-kit paired with a newer `inngest` (v4), or two separate copies of `inngest` installed.

Try this:
1. Run `npm ls inngest @inngest/agent-kit` in the example. Look for duplicates or a version outside agent-kit's `inngest` peer/dependency range.
2. Align them. Either upgrade to the latest `@inngest/agent-kit` and `inngest` together, or pin `inngest` to the version the example's lockfile targets. Then delete `node_modules` and the lockfile and run `npm install` again.
3. Make sure the agent runs inside an Inngest function (via `step`/`serve`), not by calling `network.run()` directly from a plain script. Without a function context, `getStepTools` returns undefined. If you hit this in `simple-agent.ts`, check how it's invoked.

I couldn't confirm the exact fixed version from the sources. If the aligned versions still fail, please share the `npm ls` output and the example's `package.json`.

firstDraft.whyUnsure: No doc or past fix matched this

control.text:
This is almost certainly a version mismatch, not a Node/macOS problem. `getStepTools` reads `step` from the async-local-storage context that the Inngest SDK sets up when a function executes. If `@inngest/agent-kit` resolves a different copy of `inngest` than the one running your function, that context is `undefined`, and you get `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'step')`. A network or agent run outside an Inngest function (no `step` context) fails the same way.

Try this:
1. In the example directory, run `npm ls inngest @inngest/agent-kit`. Look for duplicate or mismatched `inngest` versions.
2. Bump both to current and dedupe: `npm i inngest@latest @inngest/agent-kit@latest && npm dedupe`. Then delete `node_modules` and the lockfile and reinstall if it persists.
3. Check that `inngest` is a single version, because agent-kit declares it as a peer dependency.
4. If `simple-agent.ts` calls `network.run(...)` directly in a plain script, run it inside an Inngest function instead (`inngest.createFunction(...)` served via `serve`, and triggered by an event). Then `step` is available. Running it directly outside a function only works in the newer agent-kit versions that fall back to non-durable execution.

So yes, a version bump is likely needed. The examples pin older versions that can drift from the latest `inngest`. Node 24 is probably not the cause, but if the bump doesn't help, try Node 22 LTS to rule it out.

I'm working from memory here, not from a source, so I'm not certain which of the causes above applies. The `npm ls` output would show which one it is.
control.docsGap: The agent-kit docs and examples should say which inngest version they require, and that network.run must run inside an Inngest function (or what fallback applies) to avoid the getStepTools error.
control.whyUnsure: No doc or past fix matched this: the diagnosis comes from my knowledge of the SDK's context handling, not a confirmed fix.

title: ESM Module Error: @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod compatibility with agent-kit
question:
## Bug Description
When using the latest version of @inngest/agent-kit (v0.3.0) with Next.js, I'm encountering an ESM/CommonJS compatibility issue. The agent-kit package tries to import @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod using CommonJS require(), but that package is an ESM module.

When using @inngest/agent-kit v0.2.2:

 ⨯ [Error: require() of ES Module /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod/dist/index.js from /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@inngest/agent-kit/dist/agent.js not supported.
Instead change the require of index.js in /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@inngest/agent-kit/dist/agent.js to a dynamic import() which is available in all CommonJS modules.] {
  code: 'ERR_REQUIRE_ESM'
}



## Environment
- Next.js: 15.1.3
- @inngest/agent-kit: Tested v0.1.2 (works), v0.2.2 and v0.3.0 (both fail)
- inngest: 3.31.11
- React: 19.0.0
- Node.js version: 20.15.1

## Reproduction Steps
1. Set up a Next.js project with dependencies as listed above
2. Install @inngest/agent-kit v0.1.2 (works correctly)
3. Upgrade to @inngest/agent-kit v0.2.2 or v0.3.0
4. Run the development server (npm run dev)
5. The server fails with ESM/CommonJS compatibility errors

## Attempted Solutions
I've tried various workarounds including:
- Adding transpilePackages: ['@inngest/agent-kit', '@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod'] to next.config.js
- Setting experimental.esmExternals to 'loose' in next.config.js
- Creating a bridge module that avoids using agent-kit directly and falls back to inngest.step.ai.infer()
- Modifying webpack configuration to handle ESM modules
- Downgrading from v0.3.0 to v0.2.2 (but encountered similar errors with pkce-challenge)

None of these solutions have fully resolved the issue. The only version that works correctly is v0.1.2, but it lacks the newer features I need.

## Suggested Fix
The agent-kit package should be updated to:
1. Use dynamic import() instead of require() when importing ESM modules
2. Provide a compatibility layer for both ESM and CommonJS environments
3. Update dependencies to versions that support dual module systems

This issue affects the usability of agent-kit in Next.js projects, which is a common use case for Inngest functions.
gold_answer: The ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error comes from agent-kit importing the ESM-only @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod with require(). Upgrading to @inngest/agent-kit@0.3.1, which ships both CJS and ESM builds, resolves it.
gold_thread:
Thanks for the detailed report, @eraykeskinmac!

Could you try using `@inngest/agent-kit@0.3.1`? This offers dual CJS and ESM builds so may resolve the issue immediately.

If not, we can ship another change to handle this case.
---
Awesome! Thanks for testing and glad it's looking good, @eraykeskinmac! 🙌 

cc @MonsterDeveloper - thanks for the PR 🙂

cleaned.question: Using @inngest/agent-kit v0.2.2 or v0.3.0 with Next.js 15.1.3, inngest 3.31.11, React 19.0.0, and Node 20.15.1, the server fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM because agent-kit's dist/agent.js calls require() on @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod, which is an ESM-only package (v0.1.2 works). Workarounds tried (transpilePackages, experimental.esmExternals 'loose', webpack changes, a bridge module using inngest.step.ai.infer, downgrading to v0.2.2) did not fully fix it, and the user asks how to resolve this or what agent-kit change is needed.

firstDraft.text:
This is an agent-kit packaging bug, not something your Next.js config can fully fix. agent-kit's CJS build (`dist/agent.js`) uses `require("@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod")`, and newer versions of that dependency are ESM-only. Node 20.15 can't `require()` ESM (that only works unflagged from 20.19/22.12), so you get ERR_REQUIRE_ESM. `transpilePackages` and `esmExternals` don't help, because the server bundle externalizes agent-kit and Node loads it directly.

Options, in order of practicality:

1. **Pin the transitive dep.** Force the working version (you said 0.1.2 works) with an override. This is the most reliable fix today:
```json
// package.json (npm/yarn "resolutions", pnpm "pnpm.overrides")
"overrides": { "@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod": "0.1.2" }
```
Then reinstall and clear `.next`.

2. **Upgrade Node** to ≥20.19 or 22.12+, where `require(esm)` works without a flag.

3. **Bundle agent-kit instead of externalizing it.** Add `serverExternalPackages: []` and keep `transpilePackages: ["@inngest/agent-kit"]`. I haven't verified this one against your setup.

The upstream fix is for agent-kit to pin the dependency to a CJS-compatible version, or switch to a dual-format or bundled dependency. Please open or upvote an issue on inngest/agent-kit with your versions. I don't have a source confirming which agent-kit release fixes it.

title: Self-Hosted dashboard authentication
question:
Hi everyone,

I have a question regarding the security of the dashboard UI when self-hosting:

- Does Inngest provide built-in authentication mechanisms for the dashboard, or should we implement our own authentication layer? and if yes, how?
- Are there any specific configurations or middleware you suggest to restrict access to authorized users only?

I want to ensure that the dashboard is secure and accessible only to authorized personnel within our organization.

Any guidance or documentation you could provide would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks in advance for your help.
gold_answer: Self-hosted Inngest does not include built-in dashboard auth. The recommended workaround is to put the dashboard behind a reverse proxy or load balancer with authentication (such as nginx basic auth), and to route the event/API endpoints on a separate domain so Inngest can still reach them. Staff noted auth support is not currently planned, but contributions to the inngest/inngest repo are welcome.
gold_thread:
Currently, self-hosted Inngest doesn't provide auth. The best path forward for now is @sathishkannan162's suggestion. 

If we did add support for auth, what type of setup would you like to see? We could potentially add Github or Google auth as an option, but it would take some time. We'd also be open to contributions in our [inngest](https://github.com/inngest/inngest) repo if you're interested.

cleaned.question: When self-hosting Inngest, does the dashboard UI have built-in authentication, or do we need to implement our own authentication layer in front of it? If built-in auth exists, how is it configured, and what middleware or configuration do you recommend to restrict dashboard access to authorized users within our organization?

firstDraft.text:
No. As far as I know, the self-hosted Inngest dashboard UI (served by `inngest start` / the Dev Server) has no built-in user login or SSO. Put your own authentication layer in front of it. None of the provided sources cover dashboard auth, so this is from my own knowledge.

What I'd recommend:
- **Don't expose the UI port publicly.** Keep it on a private network or VPN. The UI and API listen on 8288 by default.
- **Use an authenticating reverse proxy** in front of 8288, such as oauth2-proxy, Pomerium, Cloudflare Access, Tailscale or an nginx/Traefik forward-auth setup. Connect it to your IdP (Okta, Google Workspace, etc.) and restrict access to your org's groups or domain.
- **Split the traffic.** Your workers and event senders shouldn't go through SSO. Route the event API (`/e/<key>`) and the SDK/executor traffic on a separate path or port, or keep it internal.

Keys for service traffic, which are separate from dashboard access:
- Set `--event-key` and `--signing-key` on `inngest start`. SDKs then use `INNGEST_EVENT_KEY` and `INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY` [3][8]. These authenticate SDK-to-server requests, not users viewing the dashboard.
- The Connect WebSocket gateway is on port `8289` [1]. Keep it reachable only from your workers' network.

control.text:
**No, the self-hosted Inngest dev server/dashboard UI has no built-in user authentication (no login, users, or SSO).** Put your own auth layer in front of it.

What Inngest does provide is key-based auth for the *API* surface, not the UI:
- `--event-key` (events ingest) and `--signing-key` (request signing between Inngest and your SDK served functions) on `inngest start`. Set these (or `INNGEST_EVENT_KEY` / `INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY`) for any real deployment. Signing keys should be hex strings with an even number of characters.
- These do not gate who can open the dashboard UI.

**Recommended setup:**
1. Don't expose the Inngest ports directly. Bind it to a private network or localhost, and expose only through a reverse proxy.
2. Use an authenticating proxy for the UI/API port (8288 by default), such as oauth2-proxy, Pomerium, Cloudflare Access, Tailscale, or nginx/Traefik `forward-auth` to your IdP (Okta, Google, Entra). Restrict by group or email domain.
3. Keep the event-ingest path (`/e/<key>`) and the SDK connect/serve traffic separate from the human-facing UI. Allow those through with key auth or network policy, since machines can't do SSO flows. Be careful that proxy rules for the UI don't block them.
4. Add network-level controls (security groups, VPN, or mTLS) as a second layer.

Note that I'm answering from general knowledge. Check the current self-hosting docs in case auth features were added recently.

title: Question about Pro plan concurrency limits (100 concurrent steps feels very low?)
question:
Hi team,

I’m evaluating Inngest for LLM-heavy workloads, and I’m struggling to understand the reasoning behind the Pro plan concurrency limit of 100 concurrent steps.

From my perspective, 100 concurrent executing steps (account-wide) feels extremely low for modern AI / LLM-driven systems. If each step represents something like an in-flight LLM call, this effectively caps parallelism at 100 across the entire environment.

For batch-style processing or even moderately high-traffic SaaS workloads, this seems like a very tight ceiling. It makes me wonder:
- What’s the design philosophy behind keeping concurrency this low?
- Is Inngest primarily optimized for orchestration rather than high-parallel compute?
- Are most production users expected to stay well under 100 concurrent active steps?
- In what kinds of real-world workloads does 100 concurrency not become a bottleneck?

From the outside, it feels like this limit removes much of the benefit of using Inngest for large-scale fan-out workflows (e.g., thousands of LLM tasks). I’d love to understand the architectural or economic reasoning behind this constraint.

Appreciate any insight into how the team thinks about concurrency and scaling at higher volumes.

Thanks!
gold_answer: The Pro plan includes 100 concurrent steps as a base amount, but concurrency is not capped at 100. Customers can add on more concurrency as needed, and teams at high scale can move to Enterprise/custom plans for the highest loads.
gold_thread:
Hi @softmarshmallow, 
The Pro plan _starts_ at 100 concurrent steps, but you can choose to add on as much more concurrency that you need. 100 is not a limit; it's the base included amount.

Many of our customers add on additional concurrency to handle the types of workloads that they need. Also, many customers run high throughput, highly parallelized workloads, but they often increase their concurrency and many teams at high scale will move to enterprise/custom plans for the highest load scenarios. 

The Pro plan aims to be a plan that works for many types of companies, enabling folks to increase certain areas via add-ons (ex. concurrency, advanced o11y/extended history, support) and scale usage (e.g. executions) over time with tiers that get cheaper as you scale. Some teams have important low throughput workloads and others have high throughput or bursty workloads and need more concurrency. As additional concurrent load requires additional capacity on our servers, we associate a cost with this.

As a question for you, was it clear from our pricing page that it's possible to add on more concurrent steps/capacity? Or not?

Thanks for your question!

cleaned.question: Why does the Inngest Pro plan cap account-wide concurrency at 100 concurrent steps, and is that limit a bottleneck for LLM-heavy workloads with large fan-out (thousands of in-flight LLM calls)? The asker wants to know the design and economic reasoning, whether Inngest is optimized for orchestration rather than high-parallel compute, what concurrency production users typically stay under, and which workloads avoid hitting 100.

firstDraft.text:
I can't point to a source that explains why the Pro plan is set at 100, and I'm not confident of the exact figure. The docs only say the max `limit` "is dictated by your account's plan" [1][2]. Check the pricing page for the current Pro number before replying. Inngest hasn't published the design or economic reasoning, and I don't have data on what concurrency production users typically stay under, so I wouldn't state either as fact.

What the sources do support:
- Concurrency counts running **steps**, not runs [1]. Steps that are waiting, sleeping, or waiting on events don't count. Thousands of in-flight runs can exist as long as fewer than the cap are executing at once.
- Concurrency limits are plan-based and enforced by Inngest's queue. Self-hosted/dev defaults are much higher: the dev server hit 100 parallel steps without throttling [5], and the default function limit in the source is 1,000 [10].
- Over the cap, work queues rather than failing. Throughput is bounded by `cap / average step duration`.

For LLM fan-out, the cap is a real bottleneck if each step holds a slot for the full LLM call. 5,000 calls of 10s each at a cap of 100 would take roughly 500s. Ways to reduce the impact:
- Batch several prompts into one step.
- Use provider batch APIs and wait for the result with `step.waitForEvent`.
- Keep the long LLM call outside the step slot.

If you need thousands of truly parallel steps, the practical route is a higher-concurrency Enterprise plan. Ask sales or support about that.

On "orchestration vs. compute": Inngest does durable orchestration, and your workers run the compute. That's my general understanding, not something these sources state.

control.text:
I can't point to a published rationale for the 100 figure, so the "why" below is inference, not an official statement. The limits are also plan-dependent and have changed over time, so check the current pricing page and your account's plan settings.

**Why a cap exists (inference):** Concurrency is a step-level resource on Inngest's side. Each running step is an in-flight HTTP request to your infrastructure, tracked and scheduled by Inngest. Plan-level caps keep multi-tenant capacity fair and tie price to usage. Higher tiers and Enterprise raise the cap, which is a normal pricing lever.

**Is it a bottleneck for LLM fan-out?** It can be. The cap counts concurrently *executing* steps, not queued work. If you fan out 5,000 `step.run` LLM calls, about 100 run at a time and the rest wait in the queue. Throughput is roughly 100 ÷ average call latency. With 10s calls that's about 10 calls/sec. Nothing fails, but wall-clock time grows. If you truly need thousands of calls in flight at once, the Pro cap is too low and you'd need a higher or custom limit (Enterprise).

**Orchestration vs. compute:** Inngest is built for durable orchestration, meaning retries, state, and scheduling. Your own code does the compute. Long LLM calls still hold a step slot while they wait, which is why they hit the cap quickly.

**Ways to stay under or work around it:**
- Batch several prompts into one step, or use provider batch APIs for non-urgent work.
- Use `step.ai.infer`. Inngest makes the request, so your function isn't held open during the wait. I'm not certain whether it counts against the concurrency limit, so verify that.
- Set per-function `concurrency` keys so one workload doesn't starve others.
- Use throttling or rate limits to match your provider's TPM/RPM limits. These are often the real bottleneck before 100 anyway.

**What production users typically stay under:** I don't have data on this, so I won't guess a number. Ask support or sales for benchmarks. Workloads that rarely hit 100 are event-driven pipelines, short steps, and moderate fan-out.

title: support waiting on multiple events in step
gold_answer: Promise.race() works for waiting on multiple events in a step, and Inngest's suggested waitForAny() helper can optimize this by avoiding re-running the function as often. If timeouts are aligned, the two approaches are basically equivalent; with differing timeouts, waitForAny() won't resolve early and instead returns null when a shorter timeout fires.
gold_thread:
Hi @oieduardorabelo - I'll answer your question in #315 here!

You can totally use `Promise.race()` too! Using the `waitForAny()` I suggested in the other thread _does_ give Inngest the chance to optimize the execution of that function a little, as `Promise.race()` requires that we're revisiting your function as often as we can.

In addition, if in this case you had differing timeouts, the `waitForAny()` snippet wouldn't resolve early, though with if you had a race with a 10s and a 20s timeout and the 10s timed out, that'd resolve with `null`.

It's small differences really; if you're happy with aligning timeouts then it's basically the same!

cleaned.question: What is Inngest's official recommendation for waiting on whichever of several events arrives first inside a step? The developer wants to wait for a WhatsApp reply (event "whatsapp_reply") or a Twilio failure (event "twilio/outbound_failed") after step.invoke("whatsapp-send"), and currently uses Promise.race over two step.waitForEvent calls with TIMEOUT_MAX and `if` expressions matching on event.data.id, event.data.target, and async.data.MessageSid, as the 2024 issue #1315 only offered a userland Promise workaround.

firstDraft.text:
There's no dedicated "wait for any of several events" API in the sources I have. `step.waitForEvent` takes a single `event` [3], and the multi-event feature requests (#1046, #1315) were closed with a userland workaround, not a new primitive [5][6]. The maintainer's answer on #1315 is still the recommended pattern: race the waits with regular promise handling [6]. Your `Promise.race` over two `waitForEvent` calls is that pattern.

Things to watch:
- **Race semantics:** the docs say that with optimized parallelism (the default in v4), `Promise.race` waits for all parallel steps to resolve. To get early resolution, wrap the race in `group.parallel()`. Losing steps are not cancelled [1]. Your losing `waitForEvent` stays pending until it matches or times out, so use a realistic timeout instead of `TIMEOUT_MAX`.
- **Matching:** in v4 you can use `match: "data.id"` when the field name is the same on both events. Use `if` when the fields differ, as with `async.data.MessageSid` [3][4].

```ts
const result = await group.parallel(async () =>
  Promise.race([
    step.waitForEvent("reply", { event: "whatsapp_reply", timeout: "1h", if: "event.data.id == async.data.id" }),
    step.waitForEvent("fail", { event: "twilio/outbound_failed", timeout: "1h", if: "event.data.target == async.data.target" }),
  ])
);
```

If either event can't be correlated to the run, consider making the sender emit one normalized event instead.

control.text:
There's no dedicated "wait for any of several events" primitive that I'm aware of. As far as I know, the recommended pattern is still **`Promise.race` over multiple `step.waitForEvent` calls**. Each `waitForEvent` is its own memoized step, so the race is deterministic across replays. Your approach is the supported way to do it.

Things to tighten up:

1. **Register the waits before the trigger.** Start both `waitForEvent` promises *before* you `await step.invoke("whatsapp-send")`. Otherwise a fast reply or failure can arrive before the waiter exists and be missed. Use `Promise.all([invokePromise, racePromise])`, or create the promises first and await them afterward.
2. **Use a real timeout.** `timeout` takes a duration string, number of ms, or Date. A sensible bound (e.g. `"24h"`) is better than `TIMEOUT_MAX`, because the losing waiter stays pending until it times out or matches.
3. **Match with `if`.** Use `event.data.x == async.data.y`. Make sure both sides carry the correlation ID, for example by passing your own ID through the send step.
4. **Handle null.** A timed-out `waitForEvent` returns `null`, so check which promise won by inspecting the result's `name`.

```ts
const reply = step.waitForEvent("wait-reply", { event: "whatsapp_reply", timeout: "24h", if: "event.data.id == async.data.id" });
const fail = step.waitForEvent("wait-fail", { event: "twilio/outbound_failed", timeout: "24h", if: "event.data.target == async.data.target" });
const [, result] = await Promise.all([step.invoke("whatsapp-send", {...}), Promise.race([reply, fail])]);
```

I'm not certain whether newer SDK versions have added a multi-event wait, so check the current docs and changelog.

cleaned.question: An Express app mounts Inngest's serve() from "inngest/express" at app.use("/api/inngest", ...) with functions: [generateContent] (created via inngest.createFunction({ id: "generate-content" }, { event: "generateContent" }, ...)), and the endpoint responds, but syncing in the Dev Server fails with "We could not reach your URL. Please verify that your URL is correct and check your server logs," so the functions are not recognized. Why are the functions not recognized, and what is causing the unreachable URL?
queries: Dev Server could not reach your URL
codeTerms: We could not reach your URL

firstDraft.text:
The most likely cause is that the Dev Server can't reach your app at the URL it's trying, which is a different problem from the functions not being recognized. The functions only show up after a successful sync, so the second follows from the first.

Check these in order:

1. **Missing `express.json()`.** Inngest's Express handler needs a body parser: `app.use(express.json())` before `app.use("/api/inngest", serve({ client: inngest, functions: [generateContent] }))`. Without it, the POST/PUT sync request can fail even though a GET to the endpoint returns the dev page.
2. **Wrong URL or port.** Point the Dev Server at your app explicitly: `npx inngest-cli@latest dev -u http://localhost:PORT/api/inngest` [2]. Use your Express port, not 3000 unless that's what you listen on. Auto-discovery only scans common ports.
3. **Dev Server in Docker, or app in Docker.** `localhost` then points at the wrong machine. Use `http://host.docker.internal:PORT/api/inngest` [2].
4. **Server errors during sync.** Look at your Express logs when you click sync. A thrown error, a body-size limit, or a proxy or middleware (auth, CORS, redirect) on `/api/inngest` will produce this same message.
5. **Production mode.** If `NODE_ENV=production` or `INNGEST_DEV` isn't set, the SDK may try to run in cloud mode. Set `INNGEST_DEV=1` locally.

The most likely cause is that the Dev Server can't reach your app at the URL it's trying, which is a different problem from the functions not being recognized. The functions only show up after a successful sync, so the second follows from the first.

Check these in order:

1. **Missing `express.json()`.** Inngest's Express handler needs a body parser: `app.use(express.json())` before `app.use("/api/inngest", serve({ client: inngest, functions: [generateContent] }))`. Without it, the POST/PUT sync request can fail even though a GET to the endpoint returns the dev page.
2. **Wrong URL or port.** Point the Dev Server at your app explicitly: `npx inngest-cli@latest dev -u http://localhost:PORT/api/inngest` [2]. Use your Express port, not 3000 unless that's what you listen on. Auto-discovery only scans common ports.
3. **Dev Server in Docker, or app in Docker.** `localhost` then points at the wrong machine. Use `http://host.docker.internal:PORT/api/inngest` [2].
4. **Server errors during sync.** Look at your Express logs when you click sync. A thrown error, a body-size limit, or a proxy or middleware (auth, CORS, redirect) on `/api/inngest` will produce this same message.
5. **Production mode.** If `NODE_ENV=production` or `INNGEST_DEV` isn't set, the SDK may try to run in cloud mode. Set `INNGEST_DEV=1` locally.

Separately, your function is fine. The trigger `{ event: "generateContent" }` is valid, though names like `app/generate.content` are conventional.

title: How to implement webhook to inform user that background job has been completed?
question:
Hi, i have successfully implemented inngest in my web app to allow the job to handed off to be run in the background

However, how can I notify my user in my frontend when the background job has been completed?

Anyone has done a successful implementation of the inngest webhook to share the code snippet or can be point to some good resource for me to do my research on how to implement webhook to inform user that background job has been completed. Thanks a lot
gold_answer: Staff suggested three options: use Inngest Realtime to push updates from the function to the browser, poll the run status through the REST API via a backend endpoint in your app, or add a final step.run that writes to your database or notification system to notify users.
gold_thread:
Hi @myhendry, Inngest has a couple options that you can use:

* **Realtime** - Push updates to the browser from your function: https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/realtime
* **REST API** - You can fetch the status of a run via the REST API. [Here's some guidance on make this request](https://www.inngest.com/docs/examples/fetch-run-status-and-output). This request would have to happen via your backend/API, so you could wrap this in an API endpoint in your application.

Alternatively, you could add an extra `step.run` to interact with a database or notification system that you may already have set up to push an update to your users.

title: Can you nest steps in a function?
gold_answer: Inngest doesn't support nesting steps (calling step.run inside step.run). Group related steps with a regular async function that calls step.run sequentially, or run the sub-steps as a separate function via step.invoke.

title: How could I add an instance of logger to the async context?
gold_answer: Get the logger from the function's context in the middleware's transformInput() hook (ctx.logger) inside onFunctionRun, because the built-in logger is internally middleware and its types aren't exposed to userland middleware. Store it in AsyncLocalStorage in beforeExecution and remove it in afterExecution.
